_comment: Hindu expansion 175-drive M: late Rigveda hymn-stories and philosophical poems (Griffith 1896, public domain).

title.en: Pururavas and Urvashi: The Mortal Who Lost His Heaven-Wife
title.zh: 補魯羅婆與優爾婆希：失去天妻的凡人

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 95, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 95 (Pururavas and Urvashi)

summary.en: The apsara Urvashi lived with the mortal king Pururavas on three conditions: her two rams must never be exposed, and she must never see him unclothed. The gods stole the rams at midnight; he leapt naked after them, she saw him as he was - and the pact was over. Their farewell dialogue is the oldest love-poem of Indian literature: 'a hundred seasons we lay together', and the law stands: heaven's women return to heaven.
summary.zh: 飛天優爾婆希與凡人國王補魯羅婆同居，立有三條件：她的兩隻公羊永不可示人，她也永不可見他裸身。諸神於午夜盜走公羊；他裸身躍起追趕，她見其本色——盟約遂終。二人的告別對話是印度文學最古老的情詩：『我們同寢百季』，而法律如一：天之女歸天。

passages.text: The marriage had conditions like a lease: two rams never unguarded, a body never seen bare - the gods' own sister living on a mortal's terms, and both parties watching for the breach.
The breach came as a theft: the rams were taken at midnight, the king leapt after them without his robe, and the lightning of the gods showed him as he was - the pact ended in one flash.

The farewell is the hymn's greatness: she says the days are counted, he offers everything; she teaches him the truth that no rite can hold a heaven-woman - 'thy sons shall call thee father' - and the dialogue founded a thousand later romances of mortal and nymph.

title.en: The Goddess Speech Speaks of Herself

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 125, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 125 (Vagambhrini)

summary.en: One of the world's oldest poems in a woman's voice: Vak, Speech herself, declares her own reign - 'I move in the rivers, I breathe in the winds, I am queen of the earth and the gathered waters, and whoever eats, drinks and breathes does it through me.' The god who does not know her, she says, is diminished; the hymn is theology done as a sovereign's self-portrait.
summary.zh: 世上最古老以女性之聲口出的詩之一：言語之神瓦格自陳其治——『我行於諸河，我息於諸風，我為大地與聚水之后；凡飲食呼吸者，皆經由我』。她言：不識她的神便被削弱；此頌即以君主自畫像所作的神學。

passages.text: I move with the Rudras, Vasus and Adityas, with the gods that surround me; I carry both Mitra and Varuna, both Indra and Agni, both the Ashvins - I am Speech, and the strong is supported on me.
I am the queen, the gatherer of treasures, wise in all the sciences: on my shoulders the gods divided the dwellings; I am she who breathes in the word, who tastes what is mixed.
The warning is the portrait's frame: whom I love I make mighty; whom I love not, he dwindles - the hymn's theology of speech is a politics of patronage, and it speaks in the first person female.

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 136, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 136 (Kesin hymn)

summary.en: The Rigveda's portrait of the wild ascetic: long-haired, wind-girt, drunk not on Soma but on the god's own madness, riding the wind with the Rudras' troop, visiting the whole world in thought. The hymn is half-amused, half-awed - the first literary description of the yogi, written by the settled priests about the terrifying men at the edge of their fire.
summary.zh: 梨俱吠陀對狂野苦行者的肖像：長髮、以風為衣，所飲非蘇摩而是神之狂，與樓陀羅隊伍同乘風而行，以思慮周遊全世界。頌詩半含笑意半含敬畏——這是文學中對瑜伽士的第一份描述，由定居的祭司寫下，寫他們祭火邊緣那些可畏之人。

passages.text: The long-haired one holds fire, holds poison, holds heaven and earth: he is seen by all and is not the wind's shape - girt with the wind, the muni goes on the road of the whirlwind.

The muni's drink is not Soma: drunk on a wilder intoxication, he rides with the troop of Rudra, moves with the gods' own coursers, and receives the ocean's sweetness - the gods do not bind him with the ropes they bind men with.
The horses of the wind, the friend of Vayu, urged on by the gods, dwell in both seas: the hymn sees the yogi as weather - moving between the sea of air and the sea of water, terrifying and holy.

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 71, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 71 (Jnanam)

summary.en: The Rigveda's meditation on language: Speech was measured out in four quarters - three hidden, unspoken, known to the gods alone; the fourth, the spoken word, is what men use, and they use it badly: 'wise men who do not know it sit like a blind man's beasts'. The hymn is the tradition's first philosophy of language, delivered as a complaint.
summary.zh: 梨俱吠陀關於語言的冥想：言語被分為四分——三分隱藏、未言、唯諸神所知；第四分即被說出的詞，是人所用者，而人用之不善：『不識它的智者如盲人之畜般靜坐』。此頌是傳統最早的語言哲學，以抱怨的方式傳授。

passages.text: Speech was measured into four quarters, three hidden and not spoken - the gods know them as the fourth alone; men speak the quarter they have and know not the rest.
The complaint is gentle and exact: they who are called wise see not, sit deaf like a blind man's cattle; the word spoken without knowing is a corpse of sound.
And the first sacrifice: where the seers yoked speech as craftsmen yoke a chariot, there the hymn ends - language as the tradition's first artifact, and using it as its first craft.

title.en: The Hymn of Order: Rta and the Turning Days
title.zh: 秩序頌：梨多與流轉之日

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 190, c. 1200-1000 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10, Hymn 190 (Rta hymn)

summary.en: Four verses on how the world runs: rta, the order, was born of heat (tapas); from it were born darkness and the waters; from them the year and the days, the sun's journey, and the heavens - 'the mighty ones set the sun's light in the sky'. The oldest statement of cosmic law in any literature, four verses long.
summary.zh: 四節詩寫世界如何運轉：秩序（梨多 rta）生於熱（tapas）；由之而生黑暗與諸水；由之而生年與日、日之行、以及諸天——『強者將日之光明安置於天』。任何文獻中最古老的宇宙法則之敘述，僅四節。

passages.text: From blazing tapas, rta, the order, was born - truth its engine: from it the night was born, and from it the ocean and the waters of the world.
From the waters and the night came the year's first dawn; the universe's clock started with a birth - order, darkness, flood, then light on schedule.
The close is legislation: the Earth's sovereigns set the sun's light in the sky; rta is the constitution the hymn writes - four verses, one government.

title.en: Indra and Varuna: The Two Kings Talk
title.zh: 因陀羅與伐樓那：二王對話

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 4, Hymn 42, c. 1500-1200 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 4, Hymn 42 (Indra-Varuna dialogue)

summary.en: A rare Vedic dialogue of two kings dividing the world: Varuna claims the waters, the law and the deep; Indra claims the battle, the bolt and the hero's portion - 'I and Varuna, we two, hold the world between us'. The hymn is a constitutional document in verse: two sovereignties, one heaven, and an explicit statement that the poet knows exactly who he is flattering.
summary.zh: 一場罕見的吠陀雙王對話，劃分世界：伐樓那主張諸水、法律與深淵；因陀羅主張戰事、雷杵與英雄之分——『我與伐樓那，我倆共持此世界』。此頌是一份詩體憲法文件：兩種主權、一個天空，並且明言詩人清楚自己正在諂媚誰。

passages.text: Varuna's claims are the claims of order: the hundred waters, the ropes of the lie, the deep where the dead are counted; the king of the law speaks like a court.
Indra's claims are battle's: the bolt in hand, the serpent slain, the wealth of the enemy counted in cows - and the young king speaks like a field commander.
The shared line is the constitution: I and Varuna, we two, hold the world - two thrones in one heaven, and the poet's riddle to the listener: which king are you praying to today?

title.en: Agni's Three Births and the Fire-Kindling Rite
title.zh: 阿耆尼的三次誕生與取火之禮

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 10, Hymn 21 and ritual hymns (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 10 hymns on Agni's births (e.g. 10.21, 10.45)

summary.en: The birth-rite of fire as the Vedas tell it: the two aranis (sticks) are a marriage - the upper stick the bridegroom, the lower the bride - the churning is the union, the smoke the child's cry, and the kindled flame a birth in the household's presence. The hymns build a theology of fire as the god born of human hands every time a hearth is lit.
summary.zh: 吠陀所敘火的誕生禮：兩片取火木（阿羅尼）是一場婚配——上木為新郎，下木為新娘——旋鑽為其結合，煙為嬰啼，點燃的火焰為家人面前的一次誕生。頌詩構成一套火的神學：凡燃爐之處，神皆由人手所生。

passages.text: The sticks are addressed as bride and groom: the upper one moves, the lower receives, and the hymn watches the marriage of wood the way it watches weddings - with blessings for the offspring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda fire-kindling hymns (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The churning is labor and liturgy: sweat, smoke, the first spark caught on straw like a newborn on a lap - the household present at the god's delivery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda fire-kindling hymns (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The theology follows the technology: Agni is the one god who is born every day of human skill, therefore the one whose favor is most certain - a hearth-god with a warranty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rigveda fire-kindling hymns (Griffith 1896); not verbatim.

title.zh: 因陀羅擊碎黎明的戰車

region.zh: 旁遮普平原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Rigveda, Book 4, Hymn 30, c. 1500-1200 BCE (Griffith translation, 1896)

source.work: The Hymns of the Rigveda, trans. R. T. H. Griffith (1896), Book 4, Hymn 30 (Indra and Ushas)

summary.en: One of the Vedas' strangest scenes: the young king Indra, drunk on his first victories, chased the goddess Ushas from the sky and smashed her chariots - the dawn herself fleeing before the hero of the gods. The hymn records it without embarrassment: power polices even beauty's timetable, and the poet keeps the image of the dawn running away.
summary.zh: 吠陀最奇異的場景之一：初勝而醉的年輕國王因陀羅追逐黎明女神烏莎斯，擊碎其戰車——黎明本身在諸神的英雄面前奔逃。頌詩毫不尷尬地記載此事：權力甚至管轄美的時間表，而詩人保留了黎明逃走的意象。

passages.text: Indra, fierce in his new strength, ran down the dawn-goddess as she drove her bright car across the heaven - the age's hero punishing the sky's oldest servant.
Her chariots were broken where she fled; the hymn keeps the image without apology - the dawn arrives late or arrives broken, and the king of the storm is the reason.
The theology of the scene is schedule: daybreak must come on time; a goddess who lingers is a rival to the sun's order - and the storm-god is heaven's clockmaker with a hammer.
